case_name: CASE OF MLADINA D.D. LJUBLJANA v. SLOVENIA (No. 2)

assessment.1. Interference with freedom of expressi: The applicant company, as publisher of a political weekly, was clearly subjected to an interference with its Article 10 rights: it was ordered to publish a judgment and an apology and, ultimately, to pay EUR 3,000 in damages, plus costs and interest (see paragraphs 17, 25 and 30). The interference concerned press expression in a satirical section of a political magazine and therefore falls within a field receiving strong protection under Article 10, especially where politicians are criticised (see paragraph 4; see no. 20981/10).

assessment.2. Prescribed by law and legitimate aim: The interference appears to have been prescribed by law. The domestic courts relied on the constitutional protection of dignity and personality rights and on Articles 178 and 179 of the Code of Obligations, which expressly allow publication of a judgment, apology-type remedies and compensation for non-pecuniary damage following an infringement of personality rights (see paragraphs 32-33). The measure also pursued a legitimate aim under Article 10 § 2, namely the protection of the reputation and rights of others, here B.G.’s honour and dignity as affected by the impugned family-photo comparison (see paragraph 13). There is no strong indication of arbitrariness or unforeseeability in the legal basis.

assessment.3. Strong Article 10 interest on the app: Several factors weigh heavily in favour of the applicant company. The impugned publication formed part of an ongoing public debate about whether B.G. could be compared to Joseph Goebbels and about the political methods of the SDS opposition party (see paragraphs 6-8, 15 and 23). B.G. was not a private person but a prominent member of parliament and a well-known politician who had to display a higher degree of tolerance to harsh criticism (see paragraphs 5, 15 and 24; see no. 20981/10). Moreover, the impugned item appeared in a satirical section, and satire enjoys broader latitude because it exaggerates and provokes (see paragraph 20). The family photograph used had also been taken at a public religious event which the family attended in public view, and B.G. had previously allowed family photographs to circulate in the media (see paragraphs 10 and 15).

assessment.4. Decisive counterweight: the publicati: The decisive feature, however, is that the sanction was not imposed for the textual criticism of B.G.’s politics, but for the side-by-side publication of his family photograph with that of Joseph Goebbels’ family (see paragraphs 8-9, 18 and 20). The domestic courts consistently found that the visual message went beyond criticism of political propaganda methods and created a comparison between the two families, with especially strong negative associations because Joseph Goebbels is a symbol of Nazi evil (see paragraphs 18, 20, 23 and 24). They also stressed that the average reader might encounter the satirical item separately from the editorial and therefore perceive the photographs as a direct family comparison rather than as a narrowly political metaphor (see paragraphs 20 and 24). That assessment is important because photographs may have a stronger and more immediate impact than words, and prior appearance in public does not amount to consent to any later use in any context (see paragraphs 18, 23 and 24; see no. 39954/08; see no. 40660/08; see no. 60641/08).

assessment.5. Relevance and sufficiency of the dome: The domestic courts gave detailed and Convention-relevant reasons. They expressly distinguished the protected political criticism from the separately problematic use of the family photographs; they examined the wider public-interest context, B.G.’s role as a public figure, the satirical nature of the publication, the fact that the photographs had been taken in public, the absence of blanket consent for such use, the involvement of young children, the likely perception of readers, and the need to avoid a chilling effect on journalism (see paragraphs 18-24, 27 and 30). This mirrors the Strasbourg balancing criteria for publications combining text and photographs on matters of public interest. Where domestic courts have genuinely applied those criteria, the Court usually requires strong reasons to substitute its own view (see no. 39954/08; see no. 40660/08; see no. 60641/08). On these facts, such strong reasons do not clearly appear.

assessment.6. Proportionality of the sanctions: The sanctions were not negligible, since compelled publication of an apology may chill expression. Still, they remained civil in nature; there was no criminal conviction, no imprisonment, and no general prohibition on future discussion of B.G.’s politics. The damages were substantially reduced on appeal to EUR 3,000 specifically because the domestic courts took chilling effect into account (see paragraphs 27 and 30). The claim for much higher compensation was largely rejected (see paragraphs 13 and 30). In addition, liability was effectively confined to the family-photo comparison rather than the broader political commentary. In that context, the response appears proportionate to the legitimate aim of protecting B.G. against an unjustified attack on him in his role as a father through the use of his children’s image (see paragraphs 24, 25 and 30).

assessment.7. Overall conclusion: Although the publication concerned political debate and satire, the case turns on the specific visual comparison of a politician’s family, including young children, with the family of Joseph Goebbels. Given the careful balancing undertaken domestically, the particular weight attached to the use of photographs, and the relatively moderate sanctions, the European Court would likely find that the interference answered a pressing social need and remained within the State’s margin of appreciation. The better prediction is therefore that there was no violation of Article 10.
